name: Specificity
seoDesc: Specificity: work out true positives from the false negatives and the negative likelihood ratio. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and…
summary: Give the Specificity calculator the false negatives, the negative likelihood ratio, the accuracy and the PPV and it returns true positives. That makes it useful for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Specificity calculator work?
sections.html:
The Specificity calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports true positives in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the false negatives, the negative likelihood ratio, the accuracy and the PPV (positive predictive value).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Specificity calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

True positives=-false negatives × sensitivity ÷ (sensitivity − 1)
True negatives=-false positives × specificity ÷ (specificity − 1)
Positive likelihood ratio=-sensitivity ÷ (specificity − 1)
Specificity=(1 − sensitivity) ÷ negative likelihood ratio
Prevalence=PPV (positive predictive value) × (specificity − 1) ÷ (PPV (positive predictive value) × sensitivity + PPV (positive predictive value) × specificity − PPV (positive predictive value) − sensitivity)
Prevalence=specificity × (NPV (negative predictive value) − 1) ÷ (NPV (negative predictive value) × sensitivity + NPV (negative predictive value) × specificity − NPV (negative predictive value) − specificity)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take False negatives = 10 and Sensitivity = 10 %. The calculator returns True positives = 1.1111.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: True positives = 1.1111 should be roughly the size you expected from False negatives = 10 and Sensitivity = 10 %.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Specificity calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the false negatives, the negative likelihood ratio and the accuracy — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Specificity calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns true positives, derived from the false negatives, the negative likelihood ratio and the accuracy. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Specificity calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the false negatives, the negative likelihood ratio, the accuracy and the PPV, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter specificity in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Specificity opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports True positives = 1.1111. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Specificity calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
